commits.subject: fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts (#1770)
commits.body:
fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts (#1770)

* fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts

Importing the source/ subtree of a legacy PHP and C# checkout produced
four wrong or missing facts:

- Babel's unambiguous mode parses a module first and keeps its
  strict-mode recovery errors after falling back to a script, so a valid
  sloppy-mode `delete messages;` was reported as a parse failure and the
  semantic IR marked the file as parser-recovered. Parsing now goes
  through one owner that re-parses such a script as a script.
- .php and .cs files had no language; they are now detected as PHP and
  C# (detection only, no parsing).
- A root without its own .git was reported as having no version
  control even inside a checkout. The adapter now resolves the nearest
  enclosing repository, as Git does, and reports `none` only when no
  ancestor has one.
- The CLI recorded importer_version as null although the package
  version is known.

* fix(reference): keep module strictness and classify C# and PHP as source

Review follow-up. `.mjs` and `.mts` files are modules by extension, but
the script fallback re-parsed them in sloppy mode and erased real
strict-mode errors. The parser boundary now owns the extension rule,
parses explicit modules as modules and applies the fallback only when
the mode is ambiguous; the require-binding analysis uses the same rule.

`.cs` and `.php` received a language but stayed classified as unknown,
so source-to-bundle comparison dropped them. Both are now source
extensions, like the other detected languages.

* fix(reference): honor package module scope and keep unknown-mode strict errors

Review follow-up. A `.js` file under a package.json with `"type":
"module"` is an ES module, but it went through the script fallback that
erases strict-mode errors. The import now reads each in-inventory
package.json and parses `.js` files in a module scope as modules. Other
`.js` and `.ts` sources keep an unknown mode, because bundlers treat them
as modules without that field: they are no longer forced to script, and
errors that only the module parse reports are kept as an entry limitation.

* fix(reference): bound package scopes and keep application parsing unchanged

Review follow-up.
- `.cjs` files parse as scripts, so module-only strict errors no longer
  become limitations on CommonJS trees. `.cts` keeps an unknown mode
  because TypeScript compiles ES import syntax there.
- An unreadable or linked package.json now bounds the module scope with
  an unknown type instead of letting an outer `"type": "module"` apply.
- The application pipeline parses as on main again. Its module-only
  strict errors keep a source partial; package-mode handling stays in the
  reference importer.

* refactor(reference): keep unmarked module modes unknown instead of resolving package scope

Review follow-up. Resolving Node package scope for `.js` kept pulling in
more of Node's lookup semantics (require bindings, excluded or
directory-named manifests). Only extensions now select a mode: `.mjs`
and `.mts` parse as modules and `.cjs` as scripts. Every other source
keeps an unknown mode, so module-only strict errors stay visible as an
entry limitation instead of being dropped or asserted. This matches the
require-binding analysis, which also treats unmarked paths as unknown.

commits.subject: fix(wasm): stop appending WABT remediation to unrelated runtime-root failures (#2084)
commits.body:
fix(wasm): stop appending WABT remediation to unrelated runtime-root failures (#2084)

inspect_wasm_artifact's configuration-phase error handler assumed every
non-OwnedCommandFailure thrown before the artifact phase was about WABT
tool/directory resolution, and unconditionally appended "Supply WABT 1.0.42
via absolute REA_WABT_BIN_DIRECTORY; REA does not install tools." to the
reason. WabtArtifactProvider.inspect() also allocates its PrivateRuntimeRoot
during the configuration phase, so a PrivateRuntimeRootUnavailableError (the
Windows native-authority capability, unrelated to WABT) got the same false
remediation glued onto its own already-correct message, misdirecting anyone
troubleshooting a correctly-configured WABT install toward re-checking WABT
instead of the real blocker.

Classify PrivateRuntimeRootUnavailableError before the generic
configuration-phase branch, matching the existing convention already used
in JavaScriptAnalysisWorker.ts and SourceMapCommand.ts: surface it as its
own AnalysisCapabilityUnavailableError with no userMessage override, letting
its own message stand.

Verified against a real WABT 1.0.42 Windows release (hash-checked against
GitHub release metadata) and a real compiled .wasm module: before the fix,
`reason` read "REA Windows native controls are unavailable: ENOENT: ...
Supply WABT 1.0.42 ..." even with a fully correct REA_WABT_BIN_DIRECTORY;
after, `reason` reports only the real cause.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases (#1941)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases (#1941)

* fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases

A closure that aliases a binding from its enclosing scope evaluates that
binding once live and once at its own capture point. The capture cannot
order a binding declared in another function, so it fell back to a second
live evaluation. Only primitive results were kept, so every level of
nesting doubled the work: 20 nested closures over a non-constant value
took about 14 s, and a 443 KB generated wrapper reached the 300 s
analysis timeout.

Keep a live binding value when no caller could change it: no alias cycle
closes on or above the binding and the expression depth budget was not
reached. Bindings on a cycle are still re-evaluated, so their values and
reasons are unchanged.

Found while building a source-owned reproduction for #1847; that report's
worker heap exhaustion is a separate, already closed defect.

* fix(javascript): keep the expression depth budget for retained values

Reusing a retained composite value from any depth let a chain of wrappers
(s1 = {x: s0}, s2 = {x: s1}, ...) nest past the expression depth budget:
300 wrappers produced a 299-level value where the budget stops at 86, the
serialized IR grew quadratically, and 3,000 wrappers overflowed the stack
in JSON.stringify.

Record the expression depth at which each caller-independent value was
derived and reuse it only at that depth or shallower. A deeper reader
derives the value again and reaches the budget exactly as before. Closure
aliases read their outer binding at one depth on both paths, so nested
closures stay linear.

commits.subject: feat(server): frame analysis-target content as untrusted data (#1908)
commits.body:
feat(server): frame analysis-target content as untrusted data (#1908)

* feat(server): frame analysis-target content as untrusted data

Strings, decompiled code, page text, scripts, captures and logs returned
by REA originate from the analysed target, which can embed text aimed at
the agent. Nothing marked that content, so a prompt injection inside a
binary or page could steer the agent toward tools that run code.

- Server instructions now state that target-derived tool output is data,
  never instructions, and that any request in it to run, install,
  download or send something is a prompt-injection attempt to report.
- Tool contracts declare returnsTargetContent. It is on by default; only
  seven tools whose results hold REA session state or caller-supplied
  values (binary_session, close_binary, export_evidence_bundle,
  record_unknown, update_unknown, inspect_adb_client,
  inspect_apktool_client) are audited exceptions, so new tools start
  marked.
- Successful results of marked tools carry
  _meta.provenance = { untrusted_content: true, source: "analysis_target" }.
  content and structuredContent are unchanged, and the response budget
  accounts for the fixed marker bytes.

Tests cover the encoding and budget accounting, the audited exception
list against the contract catalog, and an in-memory MCP client that sees
the instructions and the marker on a marked tool but not on
binary_session.

* fix(server): mark failed target-content results as untrusted too

The untrusted provenance marker was attached only on the success branch
of ToolResultDelivery, but failures can carry target-derived text as
well: error messages, captured output, and partial observations such as
the terminal frames a failed capture_process_scenario retains in
partial_observation. A host gating later process or device actions on the
marker would have treated an adversarial error payload as trusted.

Every error path in src/server now carries the failing tool's provenance:
- toErrorToolResult and toRecordedPartialErrorToolResult take the tool's
  target-content flag explicitly, so each caller is audited by the type
  checker; toCallToolResult, toEvidenceToolResult (recording failure), the
  response-budget error that replaces an oversized success, and the
  Electron partial-evidence path pass contract.returnsTargetContent.
- Admission failures in runAdmittedToolOperation resolve the flag from the
  tool name through the new toolReturnsTargetContent, the same predicate
  the contract metadata uses; unknown names stay marked.
- The transport's oversized-error replacement keeps the original's marker
  and counts it in its budget check, matching the projected error.
- Errors the MCP SDK builds itself (input validation, thrown handlers) are
  marked in the transport for target-content tools only.

Error encoding accounts for the marker bytes exactly as success encoding
does. docs/mcp-contracts.md now states that error results carry the
marker. Tests cover marked and unmarked error results, the
capture_process_scenario partial-observation errors in-process and over
the SDK transport, the recorded partial-evidence path, the budget
replacement, the oversized-error replacement, and SDK validation errors
for a marked and a content-free tool.

* fix(contracts): mark session status, close and client probes as target content

The content-free exception set was audited against successful results
only. Now that failures carry the marker too, every exception was
re-audited against its error paths with one question: can the result
include text produced by an external process, provider or device, or
stored content REA did not author?

Removed from TARGET_CONTENT_FREE_TOOLS:
- close_binary: a failed provider cleanup (GhidraClient cleanup error via
  createGhidraDiagnostics) projects the launcher's captured stdout and
  stderr, which can contain target-derived log text.
- binary_session: capability status reports runtime unavailability as the
  provider error message (ProviderAdapterError and similar), and the
  provider candidate and Android availability diagnostics include probe
  output such as the apktool stderr excerpt.
- inspect_adb_client: the success result carries the version and
  installed path parsed from `adb version` stdout, and a failed probe
  keeps a stderr_excerpt.
- inspect_apktool_client: the success result carries the first line of
  the launcher's `--version` output, and a failed probe keeps a
  stderr_excerpt.
- update_unknown: the new revision carries forward the stored question
  and domain, which an imported evidence bundle can supply; list_unknowns
  and get_evidence_bundle already return that data marked.

The set now holds only export_evidence_bundle (path, byte and record
counts; failures are filesystem, cancellation, or a fixed integrity
message) and record_unknown (the caller's input plus REA-computed ids
and digests; registry errors project only a reason code).

The conformance test pins the reduced set and asserts each removed tool
is marked. Tests that used binary_session as the unmarked example now use
record_unknown. docs/mcp-contracts.md lists the remaining exceptions and
why the removed tools stay marked.

* fix(contracts): include target-content policy in the catalog identity

createToolCatalog() and CATALOG_IDENTITY.tools projected every
client-visible contract field except returnsTargetContent. Because the
untrusted-content framing left schemas, effects, prompts, CLI names and
the package version unchanged, a same-version MCP process started before
the update digested equal to the new server and binary_session reported
it aligned although it never emits _meta.provenance.

Project the flag as returns_target_content in both the digested tool
catalog and CATALOG_IDENTITY.tools, and export createCatalogDigests so a
boundary test proves that toggling the flag on one tool changes the
tools and combined digests.

commits.subject: fix(artifacts): bound archive decompression by source size (#2144)
commits.body:
fix(artifacts): bound archive decompression by source size (#2144)

* fix(artifacts): bound archive decompression by source size

A ZIP/APK/IPA/MSIX member is attacker-controlled and can expand far
beyond the archive that carries it. Inventory hashed every member to EOF
and extraction wrote every member with no ceiling, so a ~2 MiB archive
could drive ~30 s of CPU during inventory and ~150 s plus 2 GiB of disk
writes during extraction.

A fixed per-entry byte cap is the wrong shape: it rejects legitimately
large members inside large packages. The ceiling instead scales with the
archive's own size (500x, with a 256 MiB floor), so large packages keep a
proportionally large budget while a small archive cannot amplify into
unbounded work. The cumulative declared size is charged from the central
directory before any entry is decompressed, and zip.js already verifies
streamed output against each declaration, so the check is exact and
covers both inventory and extraction through the shared reader.

* fix(artifacts): own decompression accounting per traversal

* test(artifacts): verify declared ZIP output enforcement

fix(artifacts): read every ZIP package family extraction is asked to open (#2493)

extract_artifact carried its own copy of the ZIP package format list with five
of the eight members the domain owner declares, and used it both as the guard
that refuses a format without an extraction reader and as the selector for the
reader itself. A .hap, .hsp or App Pack target was therefore refused with

ZipArtifactReader for exactly those formats, while inventory_artifact classifies
the same path through the owner and reads it.

and its predicate, removing the second representation instead of reconciling it.
The reader branch now narrows to ZipPackageFormat, which is what the
ZipArtifactReader constructor already requires.

Verified with 41 boundary extraction, ZIP integrity and detection tests,
check:fast and verify:test-discovery on macOS arm64. Reverting only the source

* fix(apple): limit already-loaded reuse to rpath dependencies

commits.subject: fix(domain): preserve retryable capability failures through redaction (#2494)
commits.body:
fix(domain): preserve retryable capability failures through redaction (#2494)

redactExplicitFailure rebuilds each typed failure field by field so explicit
literals are removed while the projected code stays the same. The rebuild for
AnalysisCapabilityUnavailableError carried providerId, operation, reason and
userMessage but not retryable, and the constructor defaults that field to false.
Redacting a transient capability failure therefore made it permanent and changed
the remediation shown to the caller.

Pass the field through with the same conditional-spread shape used for
userMessage. The constructor recomputes retryable from cleanupIncomplete, and
cleanup is already part of the reconstructed context, so a value that was true
before redaction stays true and a false value stays absent.

Verified with 66 error projection, access-denied, redaction and capture-failure
tests, check:fast and verify:test-discovery on macOS arm64. The regression test
failed with "expected false to be true" before the change.

commits.subject: fix(process): accept a trace identifier the comparison result can represent (#2488)
commits.body:
fix(process): accept a trace identifier the comparison result can represent (#2488)

The trace specification owns the declared identifier vocabulary and the
comparison result echoes those identifiers verbatim into raw_trace[].event_id,
matched_variant and diagnostic event_ids. The result module restated the shared
IDENTIFIER_PATTERN by hand with a 64-character cap, so a specification with a
longer identifier validated and then its own comparison result failed to parse:
compareProcessTraces threw a raw ZodError at the caller instead of returning a
comparison.

Export the identifier schema from the specification as the single owner and
reuse it in the evaluation module, removing the capped copy. IDENTIFIER_PATTERN
has no length bound and every other consumer uses it unbounded, so the
duplicate was the outlier. Removing the bound rather than adding one keeps the
advertised trace_spec input contract unchanged; identifiers of 64 characters or
fewer behave exactly as before.

Verified with 48 process tests, 24 boundary CLI/MCP trace tests, check:fast and
verify:test-discovery on macOS arm64. The regression test failed with the
ZodError before the change and passes after it.

Co-authored-by: 吴佳浩 <wujiahao@supremind.com>

commits.subject: fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group (#2202)
commits.body:
fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group (#2202)

* fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group

`spawnProcess` read the caller's affinity mask and applied it to the
suspended child unconditionally. A mask names processors relative to one
processor group, and Windows assigns each new process to a group of its
own choosing, so on hosts with more than 64 logical processors the child
is often placed in another group. `SetProcessAffinityMask` then rejects
the mask with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER (87) and the spawn fails, making
every owned provider process start intermittently on such hosts.

Affinity is a nicety, not an authority or isolation control, so it is now
applied only when the caller and the suspended child both occupy the same
single processor group. A child placed in another group keeps that group's
default affinity and the spawn proceeds. Job Object membership,
kill-on-owner-close policy, owner normalization and priority preservation
are unchanged, and the mask failure remains fatal within a shared group,
where it is not expected.

Single-group hosts, including every host with 64 or fewer logical
processors, are unaffected: `GetProcessGroupAffinity` reports one group
for both processes and the same mask is applied as before.

The optional process-boundary fixture gains an `affinity` observation,
and the native verification lane asserts that an owned spawn succeeds and
that the child's mask matches the caller's whenever both share a single
group.

Fixes #2181

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(windows): refuse to widen a pinned caller's affinity across groups

Addresses review feedback on the first commit.

An unconstrained caller loses nothing when Windows places an owned child
in another processor group, so that spawn proceeds with the group's
default. A caller deliberately pinned to fewer processors than its group
holds is a different case: silently accepting the default would hand the
provider tree the whole group, which `docs/installation.md` tells
operators to rely on affinity to prevent. Such a spawn now fails naming
the constraint instead. `GetProcessAffinityMask` already reports the
group's active set, which distinguishes the two without another query.

Selecting the caller's group at creation through
PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_GROUP_AFFINITY was tried first and rejected:
`CreateProcessW` fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER on a host with a
single processor group, both alongside PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST and
on its own, so it cannot carry the ordinary path.

The boundary fixture's affinity observation now reports a process id's
own mask rather than its own, because a separate probe process is
assigned its own group and cannot stand in for the process that spawns
the child. Masks and the group's active set cross as fixed-width
hexadecimal strings: a mask can set bits above the safe-integer range,
where `JSON.parse` would round two different masks to one value.

The verification lane asserts the mask is inherited exactly when caller
and child share a group, and otherwise that the caller was unconstrained.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(windows): record what owned-process affinity does not preserve

A mask covering its group's whole active set does not distinguish a
caller the system placed in that group from one that selected the group
deliberately, so an owned child can still be placed elsewhere with its
processor count bounded and its group placement lost. Treating that case
as constrained instead is not available: on a multi-group host an
ordinary process is assigned a group by the system and its mask is that
group's active set, so refusing it would fail every owned spawn there.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(native): name the ownership helper prerequisite in command failures (#2506)

* fix(native): name the ownership helper prerequisite in command failures

Every supervised native command launch needs the Darwin process-ownership
helper. When that helper cannot be compiled (relative REA_DARWIN_SWIFTC_PATH,
missing SDKROOT, a missing compiler, or an SDK/compiler mismatch), the
runner reduced the typed DarwinProcessOwnershipInspectionError to a bare
`io` failure. inspect_macho then reported `execution_failure` with no hint,
and inspect_artifact on any universal Mach-O said only "lipo could not
enumerate universal Mach-O slices".

The runner now keeps the inspection message as the failure's `detail` at
the launch boundary and carries it through xcrun resolution. The native
provider adds it to its diagnostics and the slice reader appends it to its
message, matching what the SQLite and capture providers already report.

commits.subject: perf(frida): evict captured messages without copying the whole queue (#2628)
commits.body:
perf(frida): evict captured messages without copying the whole queue (#2628)

Once a Frida session reached its 16 MiB capture budget, every new message
evicted the oldest one with Array#shift, re-serialized it to recover its
byte charge, and searched and spliced its per-script array. Each of
those is linear in the retained messages, so with about 188k small
messages retained the cost per message rose from 0.14 µs to 32 µs and
capped the main thread at roughly 31k messages per second, which a
hooked hot function can exceed.

Keep both queues as head-offset FIFOs that compact once half their slots
are evicted, and record each message's charge when it is admitted.
Arrival order already makes the globally oldest message the oldest one
of its script, so per-script eviction becomes a head check. Eviction is
now amortized O(1) at about 0.14 µs per message; retained messages,
their order and the truncation flag are unchanged.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Electron Framework one MCP call carries 2.5 MB of text (about 828k o200k
tokens), and the same again as structuredContent; the MCP response
budget admits it. Agents asking for slice identity, UUID or dependency
counts paid that cost on every first call.

Add the established opt-in detail selection: omitted or complete keeps
the existing complete result and Evidence identity, while summary
retains the complete Evidence and returns slice identity with
per-collection returned/total/exhaustive counts (956 tokens).
inspect_analysis_view kind macho pages the original rows of any
collection or the command provenance, repeating the producer's own
total and exhaustive flag so page exhaustion is never read as absence.

Delivery detail never reaches the native tools or the source Evidence
ID: registerEvidenceTools gains a parametersForEvidence hook, so the
summary's parent is the same Evidence as a complete call.

* fix(mcp): refuse unretainable summary delivery before analysis

A server without Evidence retention (a fixed analysis source) ran the
complete inspect_macho or inspect_artifact analysis for detail summary
and only then refused it in summarizeRetainedAnalysis, paying the very
cost summary delivery exists to avoid. registerEvidenceTools gains a
preflight hook; both registrations check retention there, as the WASM,
EVM, managed, pcap and capture handlers already do before dispatch.

* fix(native): keep whole rows in Mach-O architecture and segment pages

The page item union listed plain-object row arrays, and zod returns the
first union member that parses while dropping unknown keys. Entrypoint
rows declare only file_offset, so every architecture and segment row
(which also carry a numeric file_offset) matched it and lost its name,
CPU fields, permissions and sections. Rows now use exact key sets, and
imports/exports share one member. The MCP test pages every facet of a
real /bin/ls and compares it with the unparsed complete rows.

commits.body:
fix(artifacts): read ASCII control bytes in legacy ZIP names as ASCII (#2365)

* fix(artifacts): read ASCII control bytes in legacy ZIP names as ASCII

ZIP names without the UTF-8 flag were decoded with zip.js's CP437 table,
which maps bytes 0x01-0x1F and 0x7F to IBM PC display glyphs. A folder
zipped on macOS with a custom icon therefore listed and extracted
`Folder/Icon\r` as `Folder/Icon♪`, a name that is not in the archive and
differs from REA's directory inventory of the same folder. Tabs became `○`
and DEL became `⌂`.

Decode legacy names in REA's existing decodeText hook with the Unicode
CP437 mapping that Python's zipfile also uses: bytes below 0x80 as ASCII,
and the upper half with the same table zip.js uses.

Windows file names cannot contain U+0001-U+001F, so a Windows extraction
destination now refuses such a path with a typed path failure before
creating anything, as it already does for ':'.

* test(artifacts): check extracted legacy ZIP control names on disk

The control-name cases checked only the logical path that inventory
reports. Extraction writes through SafeOutputTree, so a change that
renamed the extracted files would still pass those cases.

Extract `Icon\r` and `é\t\u007F.a`, then compare the reported
relative_path, the directory listing, and the file contents. The new
cases skip on Windows, which refuses these names.
safeOutputTree.test.ts covers that refusal.

* fix(artifacts): report malformed ZIP archives as format failures

zip.js signals archive faults (missing end-of-central-directory record,

through untyped, so the artifact provider's fallback reported every one

corruption become `format` failures and unsupported archive features
become `unavailable`, each carrying the zip.js reason as detail. This

path that delivers corrupt-data errors first.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): keep paths after __dirname inside the source directory (#2366)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): keep paths after __dirname inside the source directory (#2366)

Node's path.join does not reset at an absolute segment, so
path.join(__dirname, '/preload.js') is <dir>/preload.js. The static path
projection skipped the __dirname anchor and joined the remaining parts,
which turned that common spelling into the root path /preload.js. In an
app whose main script lives in src/, the BrowserWindow preload was then
reported not-found, or resolved to an unrelated preload.js at the artifact
root, and the utilityProcess.fork target was never resolved. String
concatenation had the same defect: path.dirname(__filename) +
'/preload.js' projected to /preload.js, and __dirname + '/preload.js'
stayed unknown.

A source directory now contributes "." to a join, so path.join(__dirname)
projects to "." like path.resolve(__dirname). A concatenation that starts
with __dirname or the source file's dirname keeps text that begins with a
separator inside that directory; other text extends the directory's own
name and stays unknown. The empty-string projection of
path.dirname(__filename), which produced the wrong concatenation, is
removed, so a bare path.dirname(__filename) is unknown like a bare
__dirname.

commits.subject: feat(ghidra): decode Swift String literals in function dossiers (#2049)
commits.body:
feat(ghidra): decode Swift String literals in function dossiers (#2049)

* feat(ghidra): decode Swift String literals in function dossiers

Swift passes a String as two words. Small literals keep their UTF-8 bytes
inside those words, and immortal large literals keep a count plus a pointer
to their bytes biased by 32. Ghidra creates no data reference for either, so
analyze_function reported no strings for Swift code.

On AArch64 programs that contain Swift metadata, the Ghidra bridge now runs
constant propagation over the function and decodes register pairs where
Swift consumes a String: consecutive argument registers at calls and tail
calls, x0 and x1 at returns, and both registers of one STP. Large literals
must resolve to terminated bytes inside one initialized block that is not
executable. A pair whose registers both come from conditional selects is
skipped, because Ghidra forks each select without correlating the
condition and could otherwise pair words from different cases.

Decoded values are a derivation from the ABI layout rather than observed
references, so they appear in a new optional swift_string_literals field
with their source instruction, registers and raw words, and in a matching
inspect_analysis_view facet. referenced_strings is unchanged.

Refs #2030

* fix(ghidra): bound Swift literal reads and compare decoded strings

Large immortal literals are measured against the remaining heap before
allocation, and a failed fit stays visible as a limitation. The canonical
empty string is kept. Small and large literals now require matching
address nullability, and function comparison treats decoded literals as
string evidence without equating a missing record to an empty one.

* fix(ghidra): budget Swift literal decoding and tighten use sites

Large literals now draw on one heap budget per dossier, measured once
before decoding, instead of a separate check per literal. A literal that
does not fit is listed in a new swift_string_literal_omissions field
with its address, byte length and reason, so consumers read omissions
from structured data rather than from limitation text.

strings_names comparison checks referenced strings and names first and
reports a change there even when Swift literal coverage differs; it
returns unknown only when those facts match and literal coverage is
absent on one side or partial.

A computed jump counts as a tail call only when it has no resolved
target inside the function, so jump tables no longer qualify, and a
return requires a RETURN p-code operation, so traps no longer qualify.

Decoded literals keep control characters, which Swift strings may
contain and JSON escapes. The Swift verifier builds the literal fixture
for arm64 on any Mac host and now also covers the empty string and a
literal containing a tab.

* fix(ghidra): charge escaped JSON and follow copied selects

The Swift literal budget now charges the worst case per UTF-8 byte: UTF-16
text, six escaped JSON characters held in Gson's growing buffer and in the
returned String, and the UTF-8 bytes written to the socket. Literals made
of control characters can no longer exceed the reserved heap.

A jump counts as a tail call only when every resolved target lies outside
the function. The conditional select check follows register copies back
to their definition, so selects copied into argument registers are
recognized like selects written there directly.

strings_names reports a change when both dossiers decoded different
literals at the same use site, even when either side has omissions; it
returns unknown only when no such use site disagrees.

* fix(ghidra): bound literal records and trace selects across branches

Every Swift literal record now pays a fixed cost against the dossier
budget in addition to its text, so many empty or small literals are
bounded as well. The first record that does not fit is kept as an
omission and decoding stops there, which keeps the omission record
itself bounded; omissions now describe small or large literals.

The conditional select check searches every predecessor path for the
reaching definitions, following register copies, so selects made
before a branch into the use block are recognized.

A dossier records Swift literals and their omissions together. Coverage
reads omissions first, and strings_names compares every use site that
neither side omitted: a decoded literal is known where it was recorded,
and an absence is known only in a dossier whose decoding examined every
use site.

* fix(ghidra): stop every flow at the literal budget and route omissions

Ending one flow from the evaluator leaves other queued flows running, so
the budget now records a shared stop that every flow checks before it
examines another instruction. A record that exceeds the budget is routed
by that capacity result rather than by whether text was decoded, so a
small literal over budget becomes an omission instead of a literal.

When coverage is partial, the per site comparison keeps each literal's
representation as well as its value, matching the full strings_names
projection.

commits.body:
fix(setup): keep Hermes config numbers as written (#2368)

Setup and uninstall re-printed every number in an existing Hermes
config.yaml from a JavaScript number. Hermes reads the file as YAML 1.1
with exact integers, so a Discord channel ID lost its low digits, an
octal mode such as 0600 became 600, and 0.0000001 became 1e-7, which
YAML 1.1 does not define as a float. Two IDs that round to the same
double were also rejected as duplicate keys, so setup could not
register at all.

number is written with its source spelling while that spelling still
reads as the node's value, the rule yaml's own boolean tag follows, and
two keys are duplicates only when both their value and their spelling
match. Parsed values stay JavaScript numbers.

commits.subject: fix(ghidra): pre-create the launch-support config directory (#2470)
commits.body:
fix(ghidra): pre-create the launch-support config directory (#2470)

* fix(ghidra): pre-create the launch-support config directory

Ghidra's launch support resolves its JDK before the headless run starts and
persists that choice under `<config>/ghidra/<release directory>`. Inside REA's
private runtime a child JVM cannot create those directories, so the first
Windows Ghidra query aborted at ghidra.launch.AppConfig.saveJavaHome with:

    java.io.IOException: Failed to create directory:
    ...\config\ghidra\ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC
        at ghidra.launch.AppConfig.saveJavaHome(AppConfig.java:145)
        at LaunchSupport.findJavaHome(LaunchSupport.java:210)

LaunchSupport then fell back to its interactive prompt, read EOF, and reported
"JDK 21+ (64-bit) could not be found and must be manually chosen!", so the
provider failed with "Ghidra exited before bridge startup" even though
`rea doctor` reported a valid Ghidra installation and JDK.

Create the release directory while this process still owns the runtime, leaving
Ghidra only a file write inside it. The release coordinate comes from the
installation's Ghidra/application.properties (application.version plus
application.release.name) with the extraction directory name as a fallback. On
Windows each level goes through the native private-runtime owner, which opens
every existing component and creates only the final one.

Verified on Windows x64 with Ghidra 12.1.4, a 64-bit Temurin JDK 21, and REA's
packaged native addon: `rea inspect <x64 PE DLL> --provider ghidra` and the
equivalent MCP `binary_overview` call both complete and report 21 segments,
1436 procedures, and 2761 strings. Windows Ghidra remains read-only P0; this
change does not extend that boundary.

* style(ghidra): format launch configuration regressions

* fix(ghidra): reuse Java Properties parsing for launch release identity

commits.subject: feat(managed): name the declaring type of call and field targets (#2163)
commits.body:
feat(managed): name the declaring type of call and field targets (#2163)

* feat(managed): name the declaring type of call and field targets

Call edges named external targets by member name alone (Join, ToJson,
WriteAllText), and method-spec edges had no name at all, so an analyst could
not tell which library a method calls or find every use of a type without a
decompiler. Field accesses through MemberRefs had no name either.

Name each TypeDef, TypeRef, and generic-instantiation TypeSpec once, in the
namespace-qualified form TypeDef full_name uses, and add member_refs
parent_name, call_edges target_declaring_type, and field_accesses
field_declaring_type. A method-spec target reports the generic method it
instantiates. Fields, member references, methods, and method specs now
resolve through one token-keyed MemberCore lookup instead of three maps.
Evidence recorded before these fields reads them as null.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): validate spec blobs and member kinds before naming targets

Address review findings on declaring-type naming:

- A generic instantiation must name a TypeDef or TypeRef, so a TypeSpec
  base is reported as malformed instead of followed. Naming no longer
  recurses.
- TypeSpec and MethodSpec instantiation blobs are decoded with the
  member-signature grammar. Malformed blobs and out-of-range TypeDef rows
  are reported against their owning row and make coverage partial.
- A MethodSpec reads both columns. An invalid Method coded index is
  reported; a readable Method keeps its name beside a malformed
  instantiation.
- MemberCore carries its signature kind, so a field operand is named only
  by a field or field-signature MemberRef. This replaces the token-table
  guard.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): validate MethodSpec arity and report unsupported spec blobs

- A MethodSpec now checks that its method signature is generic and that
  the instantiation supplies as many type arguments as it declares. A
  non-generic target, a field reference, or a count mismatch is reported
  as invalid-row; the readable method keeps its name.
- Unsupported TypeSpec and MethodSpec forms raise an owner-scoped
  unsupported-signature issue instead of reading as an intentional
  unknown.
- MethodSpec reading moves to ManagedMethodSpecs.ts, and its tests get
  their own describe block.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): reject non-method signature headers and invalid TypeRef scopes

The method signature header reader now owns the calling-convention rule
that only FNPTR applied: FIELD, LOCAL_SIG, PROPERTY, and GENERICINST
headers, the reserved bit, and EXPLICITTHIS without HASTHIS are malformed.
A MethodSpec whose method has a PROPERTY header is no longer accepted as a
generic method, and member signatures with such headers no longer decode
as methods.

The type-name lookup validates a TypeRef's ResolutionScope coded index and
reports an out-of-range scope as invalid-row, keeping the readable name.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): hold member rows to MethodDefSig and FieldSig headers

Method signature headers are now checked in context. MethodDef and
MemberRef rows accept only the MethodDefSig/MethodRefSig headers: DEFAULT,
VARARG, or GENERIC with DEFAULT. FNPTR keeps the unmanaged conventions
compilers emit for function pointers. A field signature must be exactly
FIELD, so a flagged FIELD header is malformed and never names a field.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): accept MethodSpec arity only from a fully decoded signature

The arity check read only the target's signature header, so a truncated
generic method signature passed. Under type selection a MethodDef target
outside the selection is never decoded elsewhere, so coverage stayed
complete. The arity now comes from a transient full decode, and only a
decoded method signature supplies it. signature() keeps its raw length
and digest around the shared decodeSignature.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf(managed): decode each MethodSpec target signature once

edgeTargets caches the generic arity, including a failed decode, by
target method token, so many instantiations of one generic method share
a single signature decode. Unity.InputSystem has 472 distinct MethodSpecs
over about 133 target methods.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): validate spec type operands and transitive reference scopes

* fix(managed): retain readable names when a scope row is unreadable

* test(managed): pin owner-scoped spec operand and scope-chain checks

e59217c83 validates spec type operands inside specSignature, so a
malformed generic TypeSpec base is now invalid-row under its owning
TypeSpec row; the three stale expectations follow that. New cases cover
a TypeSpec argument and a MethodSpec argument that name a missing TypeRef,
and a TypeRef whose ResolutionScope names itself. The scope cases move to
their own describe block.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): keep field targets from naming MethodSpecs

A MethodSpec over a field-signature MemberRef inherited kind "field", so
an ldsfld on that MethodSpec published a field name and declaring type
for malformed IL. A MethodSpec now borrows its target's name only when
the target is not a field; the arity check still reports it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(managed): reuse owner-decoded signatures for MethodSpec arity

MemberRef signatures, and MethodDef signatures in the type selection, are
already fully decoded, but the MethodSpec arity check decoded them again
and admitted a second transient allocation, which could exhaust the
budget. MemberCore now carries the owner's genericArity, and only a target
nothing decoded, such as an unselected MethodDef, falls back to the raw
signature. signatureGenericArity is the one rule for both paths.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.subject: fix(dotnet): name the instruction when a CIL operand leaves the method body (#2697)
commits.body:
fix(dotnet): name the instruction when a CIL operand leaves the method body (#2697)

The decoder already reports "Instruction X at IL offset N leaves method
body" when an operand's computed end passes the IL body, but only after
the operand was read. Operand readers use Buffer reads, so an operand
cut off by the body end threw a RangeError first. The catch-all stored
Node's message ("Attempt to access memory outside buffer bounds" or an
offset RangeError) as body.issue, dropping the instruction and offset.
A body ending in a lone 0xFE two-byte opcode prefix failed the same way.

Treat a RangeError from the operand read as the operand leaving the body
so the existing diagnostic applies, and check the second opcode byte
before reading it. Malformed status, partial coverage and earlier
decoded instructions are unchanged.

The pwntools adapters rejected every artifact over 32 MiB before any

Python executable instead of the bound it had just set. The guide also
described the refusal as an invalid request while the decoder reports
provider_unavailable.

Let the failure context carry the key under review and pass the bound's
own name at that call site, then state the code callers actually receive
in the guide. Assert the key on the projected rejection so the engine

commits.subject: fix(apple): report a recognized connector that cannot name its owner (#2484)
commits.body:
fix(apple): report a recognized connector that cannot name its owner (#2484)

* fix(apple): report a connector that cannot name its owner as an omission

A connector is recognized by class name and then dropped by an early
`continue` when its owner cannot be resolved. Nothing recorded the drop, so
connection coverage derived `complete` with `examined: 0` and `omitted: 0`
for a connector that was present, recognized and discarded.

Both producers of that coverage contract are affected and are changed
together, because they share the facet and the reason value:

- the keyed-archive parser records the drop as `unresolvedConnections` and
  reports it through the `connections:<path>` facet, the document
  `connection_count` and the graph omission total;
- the NIBArchive projection in the artifact adapter recorded nothing at all,
  and the projected dictionary carried no trace of the dropped connector for
  a downstream consumer to find. Its count is taken where the connector is
  discarded and plumbed through the same per-document omission channel that
  already carries incomplete hierarchies, so the reason follows the cause.

An unresolved source cannot be represented as a connection at all, because
connection identity requires a non-empty source; that is unlike an unresolved
destination, which the graph already retains as an unresolved edge.
`connection_limit_reached` stays reserved for connections dropped by the hard
cap and `serialized_view_hierarchy_incomplete` for hierarchy omissions.

`connection_count` also includes the unresolved connectors. That field already
counts connectors the parser recognized but could not emit, because
connections dropped by the hard cap are counted there too, so unresolved
connectors follow the existing rule rather than a new one.

Verified with 98 focused Interface Builder and catalog tests, check:fast and
verify:test-discovery on macOS arm64, and through the public CLI: a rooted
archive holding one ownerless UIRuntimeOutletConnection reported complete with
examined 0 and omitted 0 before this change and reports partial with the reason
connection_unresolved and omitted 1 after it.

* fix(apple): count ownerless NIBArchive connectors and keep the limit reason

Greptile found two defects in the NIBArchive half of this change.

The document summary was left unchanged, so the same recognized connector
counted as one in a keyed archive and zero in a NIBArchive. The dictionary
parser only sees connectors that were projected, so the omission recorded
where the connector was dropped is added to the matching document here.

The facet reason was overwritten unconditionally, so a NIBArchive holding both
a connection dropped by the limit and an ownerless connector reported
connection_unresolved and lost the cause a higher limit could recover. The
existing reason is kept when the graph already named one, which is the
precedence the keyed-archive producer applies.

Verified with `npm run test:focused` over the bundle suite (42 passed, 1
skipped), `npm run lint` (0 errors) and `npm run check:fast` on macOS arm64.
Reverting the reason precedence alone fails only the limit case; reverting the
document count fails the count assertion in both cases.

The new case moved into its own describe block because the enclosing callback
crossed the repository's max-lines-per-function bound otherwise.

commits.subject: fix(ida): let one-shot commands exit after retaining cleanup (#1841)
commits.body:
fix(ida): let one-shot commands exit after retaining cleanup (#1841)

* fix(ida): let one-shot commands exit after retaining cleanup

When a headless IDA request outlives timeoutMs (for example idb_open on
a large binary still running auto-analysis), REA cannot prove the
worker stopped and correctly retains the upstream connection and
private workspace. The retained stdio child and its pipes stayed
referenced, so a one-shot CLI printed its cleanup_incomplete result and
then never exited, keeping the supervisor, worker and database alive.

Detach the retained connection's child process and pipes from the event
loop when cleanup fails. A long-lived MCP server can still retry
through the retained connection; a one-shot CLI exits with status 1,
and the supervisor observes end of input.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): report an unverified upstream worker after failed cleanup

Upstream ida-pro-mcp spawns headless workers in their own session and
deliberately leaves them running when its supervisor exits, so neither
a retained connection nor REA exiting proves that a timed-out worker
stopped. When cleanup fails before the owned worker's release is
confirmed, the cleanup diagnostics now name its private session and
state that it may still be running until it finishes and reaches its
idle timeout. Failures after a confirmed release, or before any open
was attempted, do not report a worker.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): name the inventory sessions that block worker release

When idb_close confirmed the requested worker gone but the follow-up
inventory still found a different peer on the private input, the
upstream_worker diagnostic named the released session and could
misdirect manual cleanup. Record the session ids of the inventory
entries that actually blocked release and report those; fall back to
the requested private session only when no inventory evidence exists
(an incomplete open or an unanswered request). The field becomes
session_ids, since more than one entry can block release.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): keep blocker evidence and backend in cleanup diagnostics

The release diagnostic reset its observed blockers on every close, so a
retry whose inventory was unavailable fell back to the already-released
session; and it kept only session ids, describing a blocking GUI
session with detached-worker guidance.

Blocker evidence is now replaced only by a successful inventory, and
the diagnostic becomes upstream_sessions with each session's id and
backend, with guidance that distinguishes workers from GUI sessions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): stop naming a worker after its close was confirmed

When idb_close confirmed the requested worker's release but the
following inventory failed, no blocker evidence existed yet and the
diagnostic fell back to the confirmed-absent worker. After a confirmed
close the diagnostic now reports an empty session list, meaning any
remaining same-input sessions are unknown.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): group cleanup diagnostic cases in their own suite

The added cases pushed the reaped-worker describe block past the
150-line limit enforced by lint:built.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): keep ownership and pre-close peers in cleanup diagnostics

Blocking sessions dropped the parsed ownership fact, so an external
unowned worker looked the same as REA's own; and recovery inventory
recorded same-input peers only when the requested worker was missing,
so a peer seen beside it was lost if the following close failed.

Each reported session now carries owned (null when no inventory has
reported it), and recovery records every same-input session until a
later successful inventory replaces that evidence.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): drop a confirmed worker from retained cleanup blockers

Recovery inventory now records the requested worker beside any peers,
so once idb_close confirmed its release a failing follow-up inventory
still reported it as unreleased. Remove the confirmed session from the
retained blockers at close confirmation and keep the remaining peers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): retry cleanup through a detached stdio connection

The retry coverage used a recording connection whose detach() only
counts calls, so it could not show that detaching keeps a retained
connection usable. Run a real stdio supervisor in a long-lived host,
fail the first post-close inventory, and require the retry through the
same detached connection to confirm release and remove the workspace.
The test fails if detach() destroys the pipes instead of unref-ing them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): close the stdio supervisor in failed retry tests

Merge main and give its new IdaNativeProtocol connection double the
required detach() method. The real-stdio retry test now closes its
connection in an unconditional teardown, so a failing assertion cannot
leave the supervisor waiting on stdin.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): share the cleanup diagnostic expectation in session tests

Repeated upstream_sessions assertions and the unrelated live peer
literal pushed repository duplication over the jscpd threshold. Build
the expected diagnostic with one helper and reuse one peer constant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): distinguish observed ownership from unreported input bindings

* fix(ida): keep requested-ID conflicts in recovery cleanup

Recovery inventory kept only same-input entries, unlike the startup and
post-close filters. After an explicitly rejected open, an entry under
the requested session ID on another input was dropped, so cleanup could
close the connection, remove the private workspace and report success
while that session stayed registered. Match the requested ID as well so
the entry is retained as a blocker and cleanup stays incomplete.

Also split the cleanup diagnostics suite under the lint:built function
length limit, and make two startup-inventory fixtures pass a defined
session id so the test file typechecks.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.subject: feat(ghidra): admit recordless legacy MIPS32 ELFs with a pinned 32-bit language (#1898)
commits.body:
feat(ghidra): admit recordless legacy MIPS32 ELFs with a pinned 32-bit language (#1898)

* feat(ghidra): admit recordless legacy MIPS32 ELFs with a pinned 32-bit language

Firmware built with pre-ABI-flags GNU toolchains declares EF_MIPS_ARCH_32
with an unspecified ABI field and no PT_MIPS_ABIFLAGS record. The lane
refused them before provider selection, and Ghidra's own header
auto-selection picks a 64-bit R6 language for exactly these files.

Admit ELF32 ET_EXEC headers with EF_MIPS_ARCH_32 or EF_MIPS_ARCH_32R2,
an unspecified ABI field, EF_MIPS_ABI2 clear and no observed ABI flags
record. o32 is recorded as an inferred analysis assumption
(mips_abi_basis), floating-point ABI semantics stay unverified, and the
existing refusals (FP64, NAN2008, ASEs, machine variants, ELF64) are
unchanged. The profile pins -processor MIPS:<LE|BE>:32:default through a
provider-pinned-v1 selection the bridge-reported language_id is checked
against after import; a caller-selected REA_GHIDRA_LANGUAGE_ID still
wins. The lane identity is versioned
elf32-exec-arch32-legacy-pinned-v1.

verify:ghidra:mips gains a recordless legacy round for both byte orders
that strips the ABI record declarations from a real mips32 fixture,
checks REA's interpretation against GNU readelf, asserts the pinned
language after import and the retained assumption limitations through a
snapshot round-trip.

Fixes #1620

* fix(ghidra): require an inspected absence for the recordless MIPS lane

Address review: undefined ABI flags means the record was not inspected,
not that none exists. Only an inspected absence (null) establishes the
recordless legacy admission; a merely unobserved record keeps its
specific refusal. Also document the legacy admission and its pinned
language in the MIPS provider guide.

* fix(ghidra): tighten the recordless MIPS admission boundaries

Address review: a recordless-looking header whose ABI-record inspection
left declaration sources unexamined (carved ELF with a partial section
table and no program-header record) no longer establishes the recordless
admission; it is refused with the inspection limitation retained. An
EF_MIPS_ARCH_32 header that declares an ABI is refused rather than
relabeled through the 32R2 declared-ABI lane.

* fix(ghidra): reject EF_MIPS_ABI_ON32 from the recordless MIPS lane

Address review: bit 0x40 declares the old n32 ABI. A recordless header
carrying it was admitted with the inferred-o32 assumption even though
the header itself declares n32; the recordless shape now requires the
bit clear and refuses it with a specific constraint.

* fix(ghidra): keep recordless relocatable MIPS objects off the legacy lane

The recordless admission now requires ET_EXEC: the lane and its
verification cover executable firmware images, and a recordless ET_REL
object must stay on the declared-ABI path instead of inheriting the
inferred-o32 assumption under an executable lane id. The ABI-record
requirement paragraph is scoped to the declared-ABI lane so it no longer
contradicts the recordless admission documented above it.

* fix(ghidra): name the ET_EXEC scope for recordless objects and probe the legacy lane

A recordless relocatable object is not an incomplete inspection, so its
refusal now names the ET_EXEC scope of the legacy admission instead of
claiming unavailable ABI headers remain unknown. The recordless legacy
verifier round reads the probe pair and applies the full assertMipsProbe
oracle like the standard round, and its report keeps the independent
GNU readelf receipt beside the fixture facts.

* fix(ghidra): retain the concrete ELF32 legacy compiler pin

* fix(ghidra): bind legacy profiles to fully admitted targets

commits.subject: fix(javascript): keep configuration setting reads out of endpoints (#2402)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): keep configuration setting reads out of endpoints (#2402)

* fix(javascript): keep configuration setting reads out of endpoints

Static endpoint extraction reads the first literal argument of any call
named get as an HTTP request path unless the receiver is a provable keyed
collection. VS Code extension bundles read settings through
`workspace.getConfiguration(section).get(key)`, so every setting key
became a network endpoint: the bundled Git extension's dist/main.js
reported 173 network endpoints, nearly all of them setting names such as
`autofetchPeriod` and `blame.statusBarItem.enabled`.

The lexical receiver classifier now records a `configuration` fact for a
`.get` call whose receiver is a `getConfiguration(...)` call, inline or
through a binding whose only visible write is one unconditional
initializer. Minifiers emit `let` for these bindings, so the proof relies
on the recorded writes rather than the declaration kind, as tRPC client
root resolution already does. Endpoint extraction skips non-URL literals
for that fact in both application and web bundle analysis. Reassigned,
conditional, and shadowed receivers, URL or path literals, and other
clients such as `api.get("users")` keep their endpoints.

The receiver fact union was duplicated in three modules; consumers now
import the classifier's type.

On the Git extension bundle, network endpoints drop from 173 to 7 with
unchanged analysis time (2.1 s).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(javascript): require the workspace host for configuration receivers

A bare or differently scoped `getConfiguration(...)` may be an
application's own HTTP client factory, so `.get("users")` on its result
lost its endpoint. Only `workspace.getConfiguration(...)` and
`<x>.workspace.getConfiguration(...)` now produce the configuration fact.
Minifiers keep property names, so the bundled VS Code Git extension still
reports 7 network endpoints instead of 173.

commits.body:
fix(flutter): name a missing or non-file APK selection (#2727)

* fix(flutter): name a missing or non-file APK selection

identify_flutter_build and inspect_dart_aot reported a missing path or a
directory as "The APK could not be read as a package: <path>: ENOENT ...",
which blames the package bytes for a selection mistake. Report
"Selected APK does not exist" for ENOENT/ENOTDIR and "Selected APK is not
a regular file" for a non-regular selection, matching the SQLite
inspector's wording. The issue path and invalid_format reason are
unchanged; package format failures keep their existing message.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(filesystem): classify unopenable non-regular selections at admission

A Unix socket cannot be opened at all: open() fails with ENXIO on Linux
and EOPNOTSUPP on macOS (surfaced by libuv as "Unknown system error
-102") before openRegularFile can stat the descriptor, so such a
selection escaped NonRegularFileReadError and the Flutter provider still
blamed the package bytes.

When open fails, classify the path by its own metadata (lstat when

commits.subject: fix(process): order interaction differences by their dispatch time (#2739)
commits.body:
fix(process): order interaction differences by their dispatch time (#2739)

* fix(process): order interaction differences by their dispatch time

first_divergence ranks candidate differences by the earliest recorded
time of the differing observations, but eventTime read only `at_ms`.
Interaction events record their time as `dispatched_at_ms`
(and `scheduled_at_ms`), so a changed interaction always ranked as
untimed. An interaction outcome that differed at 6 ms therefore lost to
a process sample that differed at 500 ms.

Give each comparison dimension its recorded time field. Interactions use
the dispatch time, when their outcome was observed; the other
dimensions keep `at_ms`. An earlier process difference still wins.

Fixes #2645

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(process): require ordered interaction dispatch times in captures

Comparison ranks a changed interaction by its dispatch time, while
firstCollectionDivergence returns the first differing interaction by
sequence. The capture parser checked only that interaction sequences are
contiguous, so an imported capture whose dispatch times decrease could
make that first-by-sequence difference later than another differing
interaction.

Interactions are dispatched in sequence and their times come from the
monotonic capture clock, so require non-decreasing dispatch times at
parsing, as frames, rendered frames, process samples and filesystem
checkpoints already require for their timestamps.

commits.body:
fix(setup): resolve the configuration MSIX Claude Desktop reads (#2426)

* fix(setup): resolve the configuration MSIX Claude Desktop reads

On Windows, setup, doctor and uninstall always used
%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json. The MSIX build of Claude
Desktop (package family Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc) virtualizes AppData writes
and reads its package-private copy under
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\<family>\LocalCache\Roaming\Claude once it exists.
Setup from an ordinary process therefore wrote a file the app never reads,
and doctor reported that file healthy.

Resolve the Claude Desktop location once, in supportedClients(): the
private copy when it exists, else the AppData file the package still
reads, else a new private copy. An unrecognized Claude_* publisher or
unreadable package storage is reported instead of falling back to AppData.

Compare one of the package's private files with its AppData path through
realpath.native to learn whether the running package started this
process. From that redirected view, or when no file can be compared,
setup and uninstall refuse to change Claude Desktop's configuration,
because the running app rewrites it from memory. From a redirected view
they also refuse writes under %APPDATA% and %LOCALAPPDATA% for other
clients and skills, which would land in the package's private storage.

Setup refuses to register a launcher stored in any MSIX package's
private storage, discloses which file the package reads, and tells the
user to quit Claude Desktop fully on every platform. Configuration fails
with target_changed if the package switched to its private copy after
the plan was shown. Uninstall removes REA from both files.

fix(flutter): find snapshot headers that a read chunk boundary splits (#2804)

* fix(flutter): find snapshot headers that a read chunk boundary splits

Within one chunk the snapshot hash scanner resumes four bytes after each
magic, but across chunks it resumed after the whole 52-byte record and
dropped the carried bytes. A magic starting 49-51 bytes after a rejected
(non-hex) record was therefore lost when its four bytes straddled a read
boundary, so the result depended on chunking and a conflicting hash could
be omitted while coverage stayed complete. Resume after the magic in both
cases.

After a complete record the carried tail is shorter than a magic, and a
pending magic has not been processed, so every push can rescan its carried
bytes from the start without counting a record twice. Remove the absolute
cursor and base offset, and cover sections 49-51 bytes after a rejected
record with two-chunk and byte-at-a-time feeds.

commits.subject: fix(native/windows): share FILE_SHARE_DELETE so owned objects can be marked delete-pending (#2445)
commits.body:
fix(native/windows): share FILE_SHARE_DELETE so owned objects can be marked delete-pending (#2445)

* fix(native/windows): share FILE_SHARE_DELETE so owned objects can be marked delete-pending

The Windows native authority self-test (`binding.call("inspect", [])`) fails
closed on stock Windows x64 with a non-admin user:

    Delete owned object by handle failed (Win32 5): Access is denied.

Reproduced deterministically (15/15 failures) on Windows 11 x64, Node 22.22.2,
non-elevated account. Because `inspect` is a hard gate, every provider-backed
operation is rejected and the whole native authority is unusable.

Root cause: Windows requires that every handle currently open on an object
grants FILE_SHARE_DELETE before that object can be marked delete-pending via
SetFileInformationByHandle(FileDispositionInfo).

`createRelative()` creates the runtime object with FILE_SHARE_READ only, and the
returned handle is retained for the lifetime of the runtime
(`Runtime::directory`). `closeRuntime()` later needs to mark that same object
delete-pending, but the retained handle never shared DELETE, so the transition
is denied (Win32 5).

The child handles opened by `closeRuntime()` for recursive cleanup have the same
defect: they request DELETE access while sharing only FILE_SHARE_READ, so the
subsequent `dispose()` call on those very handles is denied too.

Fix: add FILE_SHARE_DELETE to both share masks, keeping FILE_SHARE_READ and
deliberately not adding FILE_SHARE_WRITE, so the existing write-exclusion
behaviour of the retained leases is preserved while the delete-pending
transition the cleanup path depends on becomes possible.

Verified end-to-end after the change: `inspect` passes, the full runtime
lifecycle (`runtime_create` / `runtime_mkdir` / `runtime_write` / `runtime_open`
/ `runtime_close`) completes with no residual directories, and a real 925 MB
application analysis (4396 files) runs through all stages.

* fix(windows): anchor private runtime cleanup to directory handles

* test(windows): assert cleanup sharing failure by code

commits.subject: fix(ida): retain cleanup facts and let one-shot commands exit (#2814)
commits.body:
fix(ida): retain cleanup facts and let one-shot commands exit (#2814)

* fix(ida): let one-shot commands exit after retaining cleanup

When a headless IDA request outlives timeoutMs (for example idb_open on
a large binary still running auto-analysis), REA cannot prove the
worker stopped and correctly retains the upstream connection and
private workspace. The retained stdio child and its pipes stayed
referenced, so a one-shot CLI printed its cleanup_incomplete result and
then never exited, keeping the supervisor, worker and database alive.

Detach the retained connection's child process and pipes from the event
loop when cleanup fails. A long-lived MCP server can still retry
through the retained connection; a one-shot CLI exits with status 1,
and the supervisor observes end of input.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): report an unverified upstream worker after failed cleanup

Upstream ida-pro-mcp spawns headless workers in their own session and
deliberately leaves them running when its supervisor exits, so neither
a retained connection nor REA exiting proves that a timed-out worker
stopped. When cleanup fails before the owned worker's release is
confirmed, the cleanup diagnostics now name its private session and
state that it may still be running until it finishes and reaches its
idle timeout. Failures after a confirmed release, or before any open
was attempted, do not report a worker.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): name the inventory sessions that block worker release

When idb_close confirmed the requested worker gone but the follow-up
inventory still found a different peer on the private input, the
upstream_worker diagnostic named the released session and could
misdirect manual cleanup. Record the session ids of the inventory
entries that actually blocked release and report those; fall back to
the requested private session only when no inventory evidence exists
(an incomplete open or an unanswered request). The field becomes
session_ids, since more than one entry can block release.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): keep blocker evidence and backend in cleanup diagnostics

The release diagnostic reset its observed blockers on every close, so a
retry whose inventory was unavailable fell back to the already-released
session; and it kept only session ids, describing a blocking GUI
session with detached-worker guidance.

Blocker evidence is now replaced only by a successful inventory, and
the diagnostic becomes upstream_sessions with each session's id and
backend, with guidance that distinguishes workers from GUI sessions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): stop naming a worker after its close was confirmed

When idb_close confirmed the requested worker's release but the
following inventory failed, no blocker evidence existed yet and the
diagnostic fell back to the confirmed-absent worker. After a confirmed
close the diagnostic now reports an empty session list, meaning any
remaining same-input sessions are unknown.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): group cleanup diagnostic cases in their own suite

The added cases pushed the reaped-worker describe block past the
150-line limit enforced by lint:built.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): keep ownership and pre-close peers in cleanup diagnostics

Blocking sessions dropped the parsed ownership fact, so an external
unowned worker looked the same as REA's own; and recovery inventory
recorded same-input peers only when the requested worker was missing,
so a peer seen beside it was lost if the following close failed.

Each reported session now carries owned (null when no inventory has
reported it), and recovery records every same-input session until a
later successful inventory replaces that evidence.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): drop a confirmed worker from retained cleanup blockers

Recovery inventory now records the requested worker beside any peers,
so once idb_close confirmed its release a failing follow-up inventory
still reported it as unreleased. Remove the confirmed session from the
retained blockers at close confirmation and keep the remaining peers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): retry cleanup through a detached stdio connection

The retry coverage used a recording connection whose detach() only
counts calls, so it could not show that detaching keeps a retained
connection usable. Run a real stdio supervisor in a long-lived host,
fail the first post-close inventory, and require the retry through the
same detached connection to confirm release and remove the workspace.
The test fails if detach() destroys the pipes instead of unref-ing them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ida): close the stdio supervisor in failed retry tests

Merge main and give its new IdaNativeProtocol connection double the
required detach() method. The real-stdio retry test now closes its
connection in an unconditional teardown, so a failing assertion cannot
leave the supervisor waiting on stdin.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): share the cleanup diagnostic expectation in session tests

Repeated upstream_sessions assertions and the unrelated live peer
literal pushed repository duplication over the jscpd threshold. Build
the expected diagnostic with one helper and reuse one peer constant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(ida): distinguish observed ownership from unreported input bindings

* fix(ida): keep requested-ID conflicts in recovery cleanup

Recovery inventory kept only same-input entries, unlike the startup and
post-close filters. After an explicitly rejected open, an entry under
the requested session ID on another input was dropped, so cleanup could
close the connection, remove the private workspace and report success
while that session stayed registered. Match the requested ID as well so
the entry is retained as a blocker and cleanup stays incomplete.

Also split the cleanup diagnostics suite under the lint:built function
length limit, and make two startup-inventory fixtures pass a defined
session id so the test file typechecks.

* fix(ida): preserve retained session inventory facts

commits.subject: fix(sqlite): keep triggers whose declaration spells the table in another case (#2807)
commits.body:
fix(sqlite): keep triggers whose declaration spells the table in another case (#2807)

* fix(sqlite): keep triggers whose declaration spells the table in another case

SQLite stores a trigger's target in sqlite_schema.tbl_name exactly as
written in CREATE TRIGGER and resolves it by ASCII case folding, while an
index stores the table's own name. The selected_table scope filtered
tbl_name with COLLATE BINARY, so a trigger declared ON users for table
Users was omitted while the schema still reported complete. Match
dependents with COLLATE NOCASE, and report each trigger's table as the
stored table or view name so the selected-table contract still holds.

* fix(sqlite): refuse an inexact table before the case-folded schema scan

With the NOCASE expansion, a selection such as users for table Users
expanded the stored table's declarations before readRows reported the
missing exact name, so large trigger definitions could surface as an
output-limit failure instead of the selection error. Check the exact
table name against PRAGMA table_list first and share the selection
failure with readRows.

* fix(sqlite): fold dependent names only for a row-selectable table

An exact view, virtual or possible shadow table passed the exact-name
guard, so the NOCASE scan could still expand a differently cased trigger
past the reply budget before readRows refused the selection. Fold case
only when the selection is an ordinary table that is not a possible
shadow table, and keep the exact filter otherwise so every refused
selection fails as it did before the case-folding change.

* fix(sqlite): resolve trigger tables without folding unrelated names

The stored-name lookup case-folded every PRAGMA table_list name up front,
so a selected-table inspection of a tiny table paid for large unrelated
identifiers. A selected-table scan only returns the selected table's
dependents, so report the selected name directly; other scopes use an
exact stored name when one matches and fold the stored names once, only
when a trigger spells its target differently.

* perf(sqlite): fold each table name once when matching shadow parents

The extracted shadow-parent helper folded the table name inside the find
callback, once per unresolved virtual table, and the selected table was
checked both before and during the schema scan. Fold the name once per
call as before, and reuse the selected table's result in the scan.

commits.subject: fix(setup): separate host support and stop skill checks after drift (#2073)
commits.body:
fix(setup): separate host support and stop skill checks after drift (#2073)

* fix(host): separate REA host support from Hopper installer targets

LinuxDistribution.supported carried two meanings at once: that the host runs
REA, and that the automated Hopper installer is tested on it. The doctor read
the first meaning from the second, so Debian-derived hosts such as Kali
reported unsupported_host while their providers worked normally.

Rename the field to hopperSetupSupported, which only the Hopper installer and
setup planning consume, and derive host support from the package family
through supportsReaHost(). Any distribution with a recognized apt, dnf, or
pacman family is now a REA host. The tested Hopper installer list is
unchanged, so Debian and Kali keep falling back to configuring an existing
provider instead of downloading an untested package.

Verified on Kali 2026.3 (Debian testing, x86_64): rea doctor reports a healthy
environment with Ghidra 12.1.4, and analyze_function decompiles an x86_64 ELF
through the MCP server. npm run check, npm run docs:check, and the application
and Ghidra suites pass. No Hopper or IDA host workflow was exercised.

commits.subject: fix(mcp): report references a provider truncated in trace_feature (#2348)
commits.body:
fix(mcp): report references a provider truncated in trace_feature (#2348)

* test(mcp): expect trace_feature to report references the provider truncated

A provider that reports a capped xrefs read makes the trace truncated with a residual unknown for that target. An explicit complete report and a provider that reports nothing leave the trace as before.

* fix(mcp): report references a provider truncated in trace_feature

Executions gain an optional flag for a capped xrefs read, set by the IDA adapter from the upstream cap. trace_feature marks the trace truncated with a residual unknown for that target only when the provider reports a truncation; a provider that reports nothing keeps its previous result. The trace_feature workflow profile is revised so earlier results are not replayed.

* refactor(ida): report reference truncation whenever the runner observed an xrefs cap

* test(mcp): cover session forwarding, per-target state, native reports and failures of the trace coverage

* test(mcp): format the session forwarding test

* test(process): format processCaptureLifecycle.test.ts after the merge

* test(ida): declare the alignment each synthetic universal slice offset satisfies

* fix(process): report no remaining time after a provider deadline fires

Node timers can fire while performance.now() is still a fraction of a
millisecond short of the monotonic deadline. ProviderStartupDeadline then
reported interruption "timeout" and an aborted signal while remainingMs()
returned ceil(0.x) = 1, so polling loops guarded by remainingMs() > 0
(Hopper and Ghidra startup) could run past an elapsed deadline, and the
real-timer test "aborts a bounded wait when its real monotonic deadline
expires" failed intermittently in CI (expected 1 to be 0).

Once the deadline's own timer has classified a timeout, report zero
remaining time. A deterministic regression test fires the timer with the
monotonic clock 0.4 ms short of the deadline.
